title: The Bloop Deep Sea Sound
hook: In 1997, hydrophones recorded a mysterious low-frequency sound deep in the Pacific.

beats.label: THE CASE
beats.line: The Bloop was detected by NOAA's Pacific acoustic array in April 1997.

beats.label: CLUE 1
beats.line: Triangulation placed the source near the south-west Pacific, about 5,000 km offshore.

beats.label: CLUE 2
beats.line: Its intensity reached roughly 180 decibels, louder than a blue whale.

beats.label: CLUE 3
beats.line: Early speculation suggested a giant unknown creature, yet no sighting occurred.

beats.label: THEORY
beats.line: Scientists now attribute the Bloop to icequakes on the Antarctic ice shelf.

beats.label: THE TWIST
beats.line: A 2010 study matched its acoustic pattern to Ross Ice Shelf cracking.

end.line: What do you think caused the eerie Bloop sound?

description: Explore the mystery of the Bloop, the deep-sea sound that baffled scientists.

facts.claim: The Bloop was first recorded on 13 April 1997 by NOAA's hydroacoustic monitoring system.
Triangulation located the source in the south-west Pacific, roughly 5,000 km from the nearest land.
The sound's intensity was about 180 decibels, louder than a blue whale's call.
Early speculation linked the Bloop to a giant unknown sea creature, but no visual evidence was found.
A 2010 NOAA study identified icequakes on the Ross Ice Shelf as the source of the Bloop.
